newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO minister says resignation offers "theatrics".
newsitem.headline: PLO minister says resignation offers "theatrics".

text.p: A Palestinian minister called a resignation offer from virtually all of his colleagues "meaningless" on Saturday as President Yasser Arafat consulted with Egypt on the deep crisis in Middle East peace efforts.

Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo, who refused to follow 16 colleagues in making the gesture at a meeting of Arafat's cabinet on Friday night, said a ministerial clean-out would not resolve the Palestinian Authority's problems.
The offer from 16 of the 18 ministers was made in a letter after a scathing report from a panel of the Palestinian Legislative Council on alleged corruption and misuse of funds.

"The text of the letter does not mean resignation. Instead it says that the ministers are leaving the decision up to Arafat to keep them or remove them," Abed Rabbo, a close confidant of the Palestinian leader, told Reuters.

"Crucial changes have to take place and not just cosmetic ones," he added. "The people will discover soon that the ministers' move was meaningless, therefore I refuse to participate in theatrical steps of that kind.''
Arafat's office has said only that the ministers had asked him to consider their resignations "at a suitable time".

There was no indication that Arafat would act fast as he confronts his worst crisis with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu following a double suicide bombing that killed 13 people in Jerusalem's main Jewish market on Wednesday.

He met on Saturday with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who has been trying to jump-start Israeli-Palestinian peace talks moribund since Israel began to build a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.

The two leaders "discussed the latest developments and the crisis that the peace process is going through particularly after the dangerous decisions issued by the Israeli cabinet in the wake of the explosions that took place in west Jerusalem", Egyptian state television said.

Israel's right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has responded to the bombings, the deadliest since he took office last year, by demanding that Arafat crack down on Moslem militants, accusing him of doing "damn all" to halt violence.

Israel has also suspended peace talks, rounded up scores of suspected militants, closed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, and threatened to re-enter Palestinian self-rule areas to seize militants if Arafat failed to do the job.

In Washington, U.S. President Bill Clinton said he would send his special envoy Dennis Ross to the region, possibly as a prelude to a visit by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, once Israel had mourned its dead.

The Ross trip was to have taken place last Thursday but was postponed in the wake of the twin bombings. State Department spokesman James Foley signalled that it might go ahead at the end of next week.

An aide to Netanyahu said Israel would welcome such a visit but made clear that it must focus on security, the concern the cabinet said is the litmus test of any movement in the stalled search for peace.

"There is no other issue than seucrity at this point and if Ross succeeds in getting the Palestinians to move on this issue there is hope for the peace process," Netanyahu's communications chief, David Bar-Illan, told Reuters.
Arafat was accompanied to Egypt for talks at Mubarak's private residence near Alexandria by three senior officials including PLO negotiator and Planning Minister Nabil Shaath.

Shaath is one of three ministers named by Palestinian legislators as suspected of wrongdoing, an allegation he denies. He did not attend Friday's cabinet meeting and, like Abed Rabbo, also did not offer his resignation.

The Palestinian Legislative Council urged Arafat on Thursday to dissolve his cabinet within one month, voting 56-1 that he appoint a new team of "qualified and experienced ministers" after debating the panel's report. The vote is non-binding.
Evidence of apparent corruption and mismanagement by ministers and officials in the Palestinian Authority has deepened resentment among ordinary Palestinians grappling with economic hardships.

It has also embarrassed Arafat with international donors, including the European Union and the United States, who have disbursed $1.5 billion in aid since the PLO's interim peace deals with Israel in 1993.
